content: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder that affects millions of individuals globally and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Approximately 50 million people worldwide are estimated to have epilepsy, with an annual incidence of new-onset epilepsy ranging from 16 to 51 cases per 100,000 individuals (Banerjee 2009). While the majority of patients with epilepsy achieve adequate seizure control with antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), up to 30% of individuals develop refractory epilepsy, which remains resistant to treatment despite the use of appropriate AED regimens (Cockerell 1995). Although numerous AEDs are available, the development of new antiepileptic agents that are both effective and safe continues to be a significant challenge. Progabide, chemically known as 4-[[(4-chlorophenyl)(5-fluoro-2-hydroxyphenyl)-methylene]amino]butanamide, is a γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor agonist. It contains a benzylidene nucleus, which enhances its ability to cross the intestinal lining and the blood-brain barrier. Once in the brain, progabide is metabolized into active compounds, including GABA, gabamide, and SL-75102. Preclinical studies have demonstrated the efficacy of progabide and its metabolite SL-75102 in suppressing seizures induced by maximal electroshock, pentylenetetrazol, bicuculline, and picrotoxin in animal models such as mice (Bartholini 1984; Cepeda 1982; Lloyd 1982; Löscher 1982; Löscher 1983; Worms 1982). The antiepileptic mechanism of progabide involves direct stimulation of the GABAA receptor complex. This action increases the permeability of neuronal cell membranes to chloride ions, leading to the generation of inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs). These IPSPs reduce neuronal excitability and help suppress epileptic activity. Progabide has been evaluated in various animal models of epilepsy and has shown efficacy in preventing seizures induced by chemical agents such as bicuculline, strychnine, picrotoxin, pentylenetetrazol, and penicillin, as well as seizures triggered by electrical stimulation (Lloyd 1981; Lloyd 1982). However, its role as an antiepileptic agent in humans remains controversial. In one study (Martinez 1984), progabide demonstrated broad-spectrum antiepileptic efficacy, with reductions observed in both generalized and partial seizure rates. Similarly, a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Loiseau 1983) found progabide to be effective in treating partial seizures. Conversely, another trial (Dam 1983) reported no significant difference in seizure control between progabide and placebo. In a separate study (De Pasquet 1991) involving 59 patients, eight participants discontinued the trial, with four of these cases attributed to adverse drug reactions. Reported adverse effects included elevated liver transaminase levels in two patients, gastritis in one patient, and acute psychosis in another. Progabide was subsequently withdrawn from the market due to concerns over hepatotoxicity and the lack of efficacy demonstrated in the small study by Dam (1983). Given the conflicting evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of progabide, conducting a Cochrane review to systematically evaluate its clinical utility as an antiepileptic agent would be valuable for guiding future clinical practice.
